title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
This is the opening page (Novi Commentarii 10, p. 94–95) of E297. It sets up the problem; it contains no calculations.

§I. The elementary theory of maxima and minima deals with a function V(z) of one variable. One seeks the values of z that make V extremal. For a function V(z,y,x) of several variables, Euler says the method is the same: treat one variable at a time as the only variable and find its suitable value. Doing this for every variable gives all the values that make V extremal. In modern terms this is the system of equations ∂V/∂z = ∂V/∂y = ∂V/∂x = 0.

§II. Take a function of x and y and ask which y makes it extremal once x is set to a given value a. This reduces at once to the first kind of problem: put x = a everywhere. The situation is different when the function is not explicit but is defined by an integration. If Z is any function of x and y, the right question about ∫Z dx is: find the relation between x and y such that the integral, evaluated at x = a, is a maximum or minimum. This is the extremum of a functional J[y] = ∫^a Z(x,y) dx over curves y(x).

§III. Euler explains the difference. For an explicit V(x,y) one may set x = a first, and the optimal y does not depend on the indefinite x. For ∫Z dx one may substitute x = a only after integrating, not in the differential Z dx. The page then continues onto p. 96: so no single value of y can answer the question. A relation between x and y is needed, because the integral depends on all the intermediate values of y.

The following pages (§IV–VI) widen Z to depend on p = dy/dx, q, r, … and on nested integrals. They recall Jakob Bernoulli's isoperimetric problem and Euler's own Methodus inveniendi (1744). They then introduce Lagrange's purely analytic method, communicated from Turin, which this paper sets out to explain.
errors: No real errors. A small gap in §I: the 'one variable at a time' procedure gives the stationarity conditions (all partial derivatives zero), but by itself it does not guarantee a joint maximum or minimum. Saddle points pass the test, and second-order conditions are not discussed. This is standard for the period and only a necessary-condition framing.

ideas.what: Extrema of a function of several variables by setting each partial derivative to zero in turn
ideas.where_published: Euler, Institutiones calculi differentialis (E212, 1755), part II on maxima and minima

ideas.what: Distinguishing extrema of a function from extrema of an integral that depends on a whole relation y(x); the value at x = a depends on all intermediate values of y
ideas.modern_name: Extremum of a functional (calculus of variations) versus ordinary extremum
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744) and Lagrange (1755/1762); the term 'functional' comes later (Hadamard, Volterra)
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas (1744); E296 Elementa calculi variationum (same volume of Novi Commentarii 10)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known introductory page to Euler's exposition of Lagrange's δ-method. Its distinction between function extrema and functional extrema is standard and fully covered in the histories (Goldstine, Fraser, Opera omnia I.25).
transcription_corrections: The 'II.' at the bottom of p. 94 is a catchword, not a section heading.
The section heading printed as 'IIF.' in the scan is 'III.'
In §II the printed phrase is 'postquam posuerimus a = x'; the sense is x = a, as stated in §III.
